newsitem.title: FRANCE: Suspected rebels kill 33 Algerian villagers -paper.
newsitem.headline: Suspected rebels kill 33 Algerian villagers -paper.

text.p: Suspected Moslem guerrillas killed 33 Algerian villagers, including two four-year-old children and eight women, in a night raid at a hamlet near the garrison town of Blida, an Algerian newspaper said on Tuesday.
About 30 suspected guerrillas, armed with hatchets, swords, daggers and Kalashinkov assault rifles stormed the mountainous village of Kerrach on Sunday night, El Watan said.
They dragged 33 villagers out of their homes and cut their heads off with hatchets and swords, it said.
Security forces, alerted by a survivor, rushed to Kerrach and killed at least eight guerrillas in a gunbattle, it added.
More than 300 people have been killed in the past few weeks in massacres and bomb attacks in Algiers and neighbouring towns.

The government would soon offer a reward of between one million and 4.5 million dinars ($17,000-$80,000) for people giving information leading to the capture of Moslem guerrilla leaders, Al Khabar newspaper said.
"This measure will be announced soon by the authorities in order to wipe out terrorism," it said. The government uses the term terrorism to describe activities of Moslem guerrillas.

Kerrach lies on the mountain of Chrea, overlooking Mitidja plains used as a corridor by Moslem guerrillas to sneak in and out of Algiers and surrounding towns. Blida is 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers.
El Watan quoted residents as saying the militants wanted to kill all the villagers in Kerrach because they refused to support them.
Suspected Moslem guerrillas killed 31 villagers in a similar attack in the neighbouring hamlet Sidi el Kebir in November.
Algeria's Liberte newspaper gave a different version of the Kerrach raid, saying the suspected guerrillas doused the village homes with petrol and set them ablaze.
"Some villagers...opted to die being devoured by the flames rather than having their throats cut by...the assailants," it said.
El Watan also said the bodies of five civilians, kidnapped 10 days ago, were found in Sidi Boubekeur in the western province of Saida.

The government-appointed Transitional Council, a quasi-parliament, was set to vote on Tuesday on a party law barring politicians from using the Moslem faith to gain power, in effect banning Islam-based political parties.
Algeria's two legal Moslem fundamentalist parties, Nahda and Hamas, would be given two months after the adoption of the law to change their manifestos.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
